common_name: Gerald Darby Iris (Purple-Stemmed Pond-Margin Hybrid Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall or spring in consistently moist to wet soil in full sun to light shade; Gerald Darby is a hybrid of Iris virginica and Iris versicolor grown as much for its purple-flushed stems and foliage as for its violet-blue flowers.

directions: Plant rhizomes in consistently moist to wet, fertile soil in full sun to light shade, at a pond margin, rain garden, or any low spot that stays reliably damp. Gerald Darby is a well-known hybrid between the native blue flag irises Iris virginica and Iris versicolor, valued not only for its violet-blue flowers in late spring but for the deep purple flush that colors its stems and the base of its foliage, adding ornamental interest well before and after the bloom period. Like its parent species it tolerates standing water at the pond's edge as well as ordinary garden soil that stays evenly moist, making it a versatile choice for a water garden or boggy border. Divide congested clumps every four to five years in late summer or early fall to maintain vigor.

common_name: Mrs. Perry D. Slocum Lotus (Classic Color-Changing Double Pink-to-Yellow Lotus)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally in heavy clay soil in a wide, shallow, undrained container submerged a few inches below the water surface in full sun; Mrs. Perry D. Slocum is one of the most widely grown ornamental lotus cultivars, its double flowers opening deep pink and fading to soft yellow-pink over several days.

directions: Plant tubers horizontally, growing tip up, in heavy clay soil without added organic matter, in a wide, shallow, undrained container submerged just a few inches below the water surface in full sun. Mrs. Perry D. Slocum is one of the most celebrated and widely grown ornamental lotus cultivars, producing large, fully double flowers that open a rich rose-pink and gradually fade through the following days to a soft creamy yellow blushed with pink, giving a single planting multiple flower colors over its bloom cycle. The bold, rounded, blue-green leaves rise well above the water on sturdy stems, and the plant needs full sun and warm water to bloom well. Feed with aquatic plant fertilizer tablets during the growing season, and in zones with hard winter freezes, lower the container below the pond's ice line or move it to a frost-free space for winter protection.
sources: International Waterlily and Water Gardening Society

common_name: Momo Botan Lotus (Dwarf Double Pink Bowl Lotus)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally in heavy clay soil in a wide, shallow, undrained container submerged a few inches below the water surface in full sun; Momo Botan is a dwarf lotus popular for container water gardens, staying compact enough for a half-barrel or large tub.

directions: Plant tubers horizontally, growing tip up, in heavy clay soil without added organic matter, in a wide, shallow, undrained container submerged just a few inches below the water surface in full sun. Momo Botan is one of the most popular dwarf lotus cultivars for container water gardening, staying compact enough to grow well in a half-barrel, large tub, or small pond rather than requiring the expansive space many lotus varieties need, while still producing its full share of double, rounded, rich pink bowl-shaped flowers over rounded blue-green leaves. Its manageable size makes it accessible to gardeners without a full pond who still want to grow lotus. Feed with aquatic plant fertilizer tablets during the growing season, and in zones with hard winter freezes, move the container to a frost-free space or sink it below the ice line for winter protection.
sources: International Waterlily and Water Gardening Society

common_name: Texas Dawn Water Lily (Vigorous Louisiana-Bred Hardy Yellow Water Lily)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in heavy clay soil in a wide, shallow container submerged 12-24 inches below the water surface in full sun; Texas Dawn, bred by Louisiana hybridizer Kenneth Landon, is an exceptionally vigorous hardy yellow water lily well suited to the Gulf South.

directions: Plant rhizomes in heavy clay soil in a wide, shallow container submerged 12-24 inches below the water surface in full sun. Texas Dawn, bred by Louisiana water lily hybridizer Kenneth Landon, is a vigorous hardy water lily producing large, bright yellow, star-shaped flowers held above the water on strong stems, with a growth habit exceptionally well suited to the heat and long growing season of Gulf South ponds. Its regional breeding gives it particularly strong performance in warm Southern water gardens compared with some hardy water lily cultivars developed for cooler climates. Divide rhizomes every two to three years when they crowd their container, and feed during the growing season with aquatic plant fertilizer tablets pushed into the soil for the best bloom.
sources: International Waterlily and Water Gardening Society
